summary: This informational memo registers two media types, application/dns and text/dns. The first labels data in a detached binary DNS format, and the second labels DNS master files of the kind described in RFC 1035. The registrations let other protocols identify such content.

eli5.summary: When you send a file, it helps to put a label on it saying what kind of thing it is. This document makes two such labels for DNS data.

questions: what is the application/dns media type
media type for dns master files
what is the text/dns mime type
how to identify dns format in http or email
subtitle: MIME types for DNS data in binary and text formats

tldr.problem: DNS data can be stored in two different formats (a binary detached format and text master files), but without a standard way to label them, it is hard for applications to know which format they are receiving.
tldr.mechanism: Register two MIME media types: application/dns for the binary detached format and text/dns for master files.
tldr.outcome: DNS-related applications can now use standard Content-Type headers to identify and correctly process DNS data regardless of transport mechanism.

today: RFC 4027 successfully registered the application/dns and text/dns media types with IANA, and these registrations remain in effect. The media types are used in DNS-related applications and tools to identify the format of DNS data. They are particularly useful in scenarios where DNS data is exchanged via HTTP, email, or other protocols that support MIME types, allowing applications to automatically determine the correct parser to use.

sections.title: DNS Data Formats
sections.content:
DNS information is traditionally stored in text files called master files or zone files, whose format is defined in RFC 1035. A zone file is human-readable and contains DNS records in text form, with each record on a line. However, DNS data can also be stored in a detached format, which is a binary encoding intended for archiving and other purposes, as described in RFC 2540.

The detached format encodes DNS data in its wire format, the same binary representation used when DNS queries and responses travel over the network. This format is more compact and unambiguous than the text format, but it is not human-readable. Applications that work with DNS data need to know which format they are dealing with, so they can parse it correctly. This document solves that problem by registering official MIME media types for both formats.
sections.eli5: DNS information can be written as human-readable text (like a phone book you can read), or as binary code (like a computer's internal notes). When you send one of these files, you need to say which kind it is so the receiver knows how to read it.

sections.title: The application/dns Media Type
sections.content:
The application/dns media type is registered for the detached DNS format defined in RFC 2540. This format is a binary encoding of DNS resource records, identical to the format used in DNS protocol messages. It is used when DNS data needs to be archived, exchanged, or processed in a well-defined, unambiguous way.

The registration specifies that data with this media type must be transferred without modification. The encoding is binary, so text-oriented transport encodings (like Base64 or quoted-printable) should generally not be used, as they would expand the data and lose the efficiency advantage of the binary format. Applications that use this media type include DNS software, tools that manage certificates stored in DNS (using DNS record types like CERT, TLSA, or CAA), and DNS-related management tools. The MIME type has no required or optional parameters.
sections.eli5: application/dns is a label meaning 'this is DNS data in binary format, the same way it travels over the network.' Send it as-is, do not translate it to text.

sections.title: The text/dns Media Type
sections.content:
The text/dns media type is registered for DNS master files, the human-readable text format defined in RFC 1035. A master file is a line-oriented text file where each line contains a DNS resource record. Master files are the standard format for configuring DNS servers and for exporting or importing zone data.

The registration notes that master files are generally ASCII text, but non-ASCII octet values may occur in master files and are treated as opaque by DNS software. These can be encoded using the backslash-DDD notation (for example, "\065" for the character with octet value 65). When transferring master files, the text/dns type should be used, allowing the transport mechanism to handle it as text and preserving line endings appropriately. There are interoperability concerns with master files, because many DNS server vendors support their own extensions to the format, and non-ASCII data in comments may have been encoded in locally chosen character sets. To achieve interoperability, the RFC recommends using the standard format and the backslash-DDD encoding for non-ASCII octets.
sections.eli5: text/dns is a label meaning 'this is a DNS zone file you can read as text.' It is the format system administrators use to edit DNS records by hand.

sections.title: Security of DNS Data
sections.content:
Both DNS formats can carry security-relevant data. DNS records can be signed using DNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC, RFC 2535) to provide authentication and integrity. Certificates can be stored in DNS (RFC 2538) and are themselves security-relevant. Additionally, special records like TLSA (Transport Layer Security Authentication) and CAA (Certification Authority Authorization) directly affect which certificates are trusted for a domain.

The RFC notes that DNS data may be secured further using standard techniques such as OpenPGP (RFC 2440) or the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS, RFC 3852), but this is outside the scope of the media type registration. The registration itself does not add security beyond what is documented in the respective RFCs for the formats. Applications that transport or process DNS data should apply appropriate security measures based on the sensitivity of the data being handled.
sections.eli5: DNS data can contain secrets and important trust information. You should encrypt DNS files if they are sensitive, using tools like PGP. The labels themselves do not provide security; they just identify what kind of data you have.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: This RFC formally registers the two media types with IANA following the procedures defined in RFC 2048. The registrations were completed with IANA in 2005. These media types can now be used in Content-Type headers in HTTP, email, and other protocols that support MIME types. When a DNS-related tool receives a file labeled with application/dns or text/dns, it can immediately determine how to parse the content.
sections.eli5: This memo fills out the official paperwork to make these labels official. After this, you can use them in emails and on websites to say 'this is a DNS file.'
